newsitem.title: THAILAND: New Thai finmin faces daunting task-analysts.
newsitem.headline: New Thai finmin faces daunting task-analysts.

text.p: Thailand's new finance minister Thanong Bidaya faces a daunting task trying to salvage the country's crisis-ridden economy, economists and analysts said on Friday.

Thanong, a top executive at a medium-sized bank, will have to handle an economy at its weakest point in more than a decade and as a lesser-known personality will have to work hard to win the confidence of ailing markets, they told Reuters.

First of all, he would have to prove he has enough independence to handle his policy without political interference while paradoxically having to depend on the support of politicians and bureaucrats to get things done, they said.
"It is a concern whether he will face the same fate that Amnuay had faced," said Arporn Chewakrenkai, chief economist of Deutsche Morgan Grenfrell.
His predecessor, Amnuay Viravan, a respected non-elected minister, was embattled by political infighting and stepped down on Thursday.
Integrity was one of the issues raised by analysts.

Thanong was president of Thai Military Bank before he took up the job. Although rated as the sixth-largest commercial bank, TMB, like many financial institutions, was rattled by rising non-performing loan problems, analysts said.
"He must show us that he has no vested interest and can pursue his financial policy with independence and integrity," said another analyst from a British investment bank.
Handling Thailand's economy at this critical time will be a thankless job and will pose a tremendous challenge for him, the analysts said.

Thailand's economy is undergoing a severe downturn, exports have turned sluggish, the ailing finance sector is over-exposed to depressed property firms, the stock market is at an eight year low, and tight liquidity has aggravated the problems.
Market players were cautious, saying they wanted to see clear direction that Thanong will take the helm of the powerful finance ministry.

There were concerns in the money market about the future of Thailand's policy of stoutly defending the baht which Amnuay took seriously. Analysts wondered what Thanong's stand would be but Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh made it clear on Thursday that his government would follow Amnuay's policy.
"The offshore market is a little bit cautious because Thanong apparently has quite a low profile among the Thai bankers," Andy Tan, general manager at Singapore-based MMS International, told Reuters.
"This is because the market was not quite sure how the future direction of Thai economic policies are going to be."
The stock market, on the other hand, reacted positively and ended 3.3 percent higher after closing at a 98-month low on Thursday.

"We don't see real buying signals from our local and foreign investors. The gains look suspiciously like a smokescreen that can easily evaporate. We advised our clients to stay on the sidelines," said a marketing head of a major Thai brokerage firm, who declined to be named.
But brokers said the rise was a reflection of a sign of relief that uncertainty had cleared.
